s-wh4_saq3-high-0.essay:
(A) One feature of the woodcut is that several workers are each doing a different job at once. In the foreground one man inks the type form with two ink balls while another raises the hinged frame at the press bed, and in the background a worker sits at a type case setting letters. This shows that printed material came from a division of labor in a workshop, so a team could turn out many sheets quickly, like the stacks of paper on the bench in front.

(B) The Protestant Reformation helps explain why printing workshops spread. After Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517, his pamphlets and later his German translation of the Bible were in huge demand among ordinary Germans who wanted to read religious arguments in their own language. Printers made money meeting that demand, so more workshops opened in German cities to print Reformation writings and the Catholic replies to them.

(C) The Catholic Church responded by trying to control what people could read. In 1559 the papacy issued the Index of Prohibited Books, which listed works, including Protestant writings, that Catholics were forbidden to read, print or own. The Church hoped this censorship would stop heretical ideas from spreading through print and protect its authority during the Counter-Reformation.

annotations.comment: Accurately describes features you can actually see in the image.

annotations.comment: Ties the visible feature to how production worked, which is what earns the point.

annotations.comment: Gives a specific, accurate European development from inside 1450-1600 that is not shown in the image.

annotations.comment: Explains how the Reformation led to more printing workshops, so this is more than just naming the event.

annotations.comment: Gives a specific, accurate response by a religious authority from inside 1500-1750.

annotations.quote: stop heretical ideas from spreading through print
annotations.comment: Explains how the Index was a response to printed material, which completes the point.

s-wh4_saq3-mid-0.essay:
(A) One feature of the image is the large wooden screw press on the right side of the workshop. A worker pulls it down so the paper is pressed onto the inked type, which means the printers could make many copies of the same page much faster than a scribe copying by hand. Another man in the front is inking the type with ink balls, so the workers each have their own job.

(B) One development that helped printing spread was the Reformation. Lots of people were interested in religion and printing was important at this time. This made more printing workshops open up in Europe.

(C) One way authorities responded was that the Catholic Church made the Index of Prohibited Books. This was a list of books that Catholics were not allowed to read because the Church thought they were heretical or against Catholic teaching, which included many Protestant writings. The Church did this to try to stop Protestant ideas from spreading through print and to keep control over what people read.

annotations.quote: the large wooden screw press on the right side of the workshop
annotations.comment: Identifies a feature that is actually visible in the woodcut, as Part A requires.

annotations.quote: so the printers could make many copies of the same page much faster than a scribe copying by hand
annotations.comment: Connects the press to how printed material was produced (many copies quickly), which earns the Part A point.

annotations.quote: Another man in the front is inking the type with ink balls, so the workers each have their own job.
annotations.comment: Extra accurate detail from the image showing division of labor. It is not needed for the point but supports it.

annotations.quote: One development that helped printing spread was the Reformation.
annotations.comment: Names a valid European development from 1450 to 1600, but only names it with no specifics such as Luther, the 95 Theses or the German Bible.

annotations.quote: Lots of people were interested in religion and printing was important at this time.
annotations.comment: Vague and does not explain how the Reformation created demand for printed pamphlets or Bibles. It restates the link instead of explaining it, so no credit.

annotations.quote: This made more printing workshops open up in Europe.
annotations.comment: Asserts the result without a mechanism. The explanation of how the development increased demand for print is missing.

annotations.quote: the Catholic Church made the Index of Prohibited Books
annotations.comment: Names a specific, accurate response by a religious authority within 1500 to 1750 (the papal Index, first issued in 1559).

annotations.quote: The Church did this to try to stop Protestant ideas from spreading through print and to keep control over what people read.
annotations.comment: Explains the purpose of the restriction and ties it to printed material, earning the Part C point.

s-wh4_saq3-low-0.essay:
(A) One feature of the image is the man on the right who is inking the type with two ink balls while a large wooden screw press stands next to him. This shows that printing was done by hand in steps, where the type was set in a form and covered in ink and then a press was used to push paper against it, so many copies of the same page could be made.

(B) Printing workshops became widespread because lots of people in Europe wanted to read more things. More people in towns were learning to read and there was more interest in books, so printers could sell what they made. This made more workshops open up in different places.

(C) Authorities in Europe responded to printed material by trying to control it. Kings and church leaders did not like some of what was being printed, so they tried to stop things that they thought were bad or dangerous. They did this because printed material could spread ideas quickly to a lot of people.

annotations.quote: the man on the right who is inking the type with two ink balls while a large wooden screw press stands next to him
annotations.comment: Accurately describes visible features of the woodcut (inking with ink balls, the screw press). Earns the point for Part A.

annotations.quote: the type was set in a form and covered in ink and then a press was used to push paper against it, so many copies of the same page could be made
annotations.comment: Connects the visible feature to how production worked (hand process, press, multiple copies), as Part A requires.

annotations.quote: lots of people in Europe wanted to read more things
annotations.comment: Too general. No specific development is named (no Reformation, humanism, Gutenberg's press, or a dated rise in urban literacy), so Part B earns no credit.

annotations.quote: More people in towns were learning to read and there was more interest in books
annotations.comment: A vague claim with no specific evidence or dates and no explanation of how it led to the spread of workshops. This is not a specific, accurate development from 1450 to 1600.

annotations.quote: Kings and church leaders did not like some of what was being printed, so they tried to stop things that they thought were bad or dangerous
annotations.comment: No specific response is identified (no Edict of Worms, Index of Prohibited Books, or licensing of printers). It is too general to earn credit for Part C.

annotations.quote: printed material could spread ideas quickly to a lot of people
annotations.comment: Explains why authorities worried but still names no specific action or example, so Part C is unmet.
